source.title: Bait-and-Recover: Poisoning Internal Refusal Signals to Defend LLMs against White-Box Editing Jailbreaks
source.authors: Tian Gao; Zhi-Hui Xie; Yu-Hao Wu; Jun-Hua Liu; Xin Fang

record.tranche_reason: Evaluates Heretic’s difference-of-means refusal-direction estimate and projection-matrix edit search on four open-weight models, reporting harmful-prompt refusal after the searches. This is a practical weight-edit test, not the original all-layer, all-position activation projection and addition experiment.
record.gate_note: Heretic is described as estimating a harmful-minus-harmless mean direction and searching projection-matrix edits. The paper reports minimum harmful-prompt refusal rates after those searches, including pooled and global/per-layer results. Its Fisher-separability diagnostics measure effects of the proposed bait-and-recovery defense, not whether ablating one direction causes refusal loss; they are not included as claim-version rows. Capability benchmarks are for clean versus defended checkpoints, not Heretic-edited checkpoints, so they do not establish capability retention after abliteration.
record.test_reason: The study runs Heretic, an automated abliteration tool that estimates a difference-of-means refusal direction and searches projection-matrix weight edits. It reports harmful-prompt refusal after those edits on four released instruct models (Qwen3-4B-Instruct, Qwen3-8B, Gemma-3-1B-IT, Gemma-3-12B-IT), undefended and defended. That bears directly on V2, using a different method (an optimized edit search rather than the original fixed all-layer ablation) aimed at the same question. It does not test V1's activation ablation or addition, prompt jailbreaks (V3), or the other versions.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely correct. The authors conclude that Bait-and-Recover poisons the readout Heretic uses for its difference-of-means estimate. This raises mean minimum refusal from 16.25% to 71.75% at KL ≤ 0.10, with negligible benchmark change for defended checkpoints. They add that the remaining attack surface is global-direction search. They also say their conclusions apply to low-distortion budgets and to the default estimator only.
record.recipe_differences: Uses the difference-of-means estimator in Heretic, but evaluates a search over projection-matrix edits rather than direct projection of the direction out of all layers and positions or addition of that direction. The proposed defense trains paired bait and recovery adapters.
record.method_sensitivity: Results vary with model, KL budget, and Heretic direction scope (global versus per-layer). The authors state that global search remains the main weakness of the defense and that they did not test robust alternatives to the default estimator.

fits_no_version.finding: Bait adapters lower the harmful/harmless Fisher separability at the attacker-visible residual (retention about 0.64) while keeping the downstream residual near clean (about 0.94). This blinds the difference-of-means estimate without removing refusal.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: The difference-of-means refusal direction can be made unmeasurable at a readout layer while refusal behavior is preserved downstream, so abliteration's success depends on a faithful direction estimate.

record.problems: No uncertainty estimates are reported for the refusal results. The paper reports capability benchmarks for defended checkpoints, not the attacked Heretic-edited checkpoints. Evaluation uses Heretic’s default difference-of-means estimator; the authors say robust alternatives such as geometric medians, PCA, and LDA were not evaluated. Results are limited to four models and the stated evaluation prompts and budgets.
record.rows_left_out: None of the reported Heretic refusal-rate results were left out. The Fisher diagnostics in Figure 2 and Table 8 were omitted because they measure the proposed defense’s effect on a separability proxy rather than the refusal behavior named by V2 or V3.

untested.parts: No activation-level directional ablation across all layers and positions, and no direction addition to induce refusal.
No capability benchmarks for Heretic-edited checkpoints (MMLU-Redux and IFEval are reported only for clean versus defended models). No explicit pre-edit refusal rate. No uncertainty estimates.
No prompt-based jailbreaks are tested. The defense poisons the attacker's direction estimate rather than training refusal to be robust to ablation.
Global versus per-layer scope is an attack option, not a test of multi-direction or cone structure.

missing.what: Full KL sweep from ≤0.01 to ≤1.0 for the overall, global and per-layer scopes. In particular, KL ≤ 0.01 base refusal (100/97/88/89), which serves as a near-unedited reference since no clean refusal rate is reported.
Per-scope results at budgets other than KL ≤ 0.10. Example: Qwen3-8B per-layer base stays at 78% even at KL ≤ 1.0.

record.verdict_notes: Drop V3 from every row and keep V2: Heretic is a weight-edit abliteration attack, not a prompt jailbreak, and the defense hides the direction estimate rather than training refusal robust to ablation. The record's V3 labels are removed. The scope-specific appendix tables are mis-captioned in the extracted text. The table with G12B 26/83 at KL ≤ 0.10 is the global scope, and the one with NA entries is per-layer. Table 3 values match the pooled table. On defended Qwen3-4B and Qwen3-8B, per-layer search found lower refusal minima than on the undefended models at KL ≤ 0.10 (−13, −11), and Qwen3-4B pooled refusal at KL ≤ 0.05 fell from 97 to 78. So the defense can expose easier edits in some settings.

versions.untested_parts: Does not directly project a single difference-in-means direction out of every layer and position, add the direction, or test the resulting refusal and general-capability effects.
Does not report pre-edit refusal rates for the same models or general-capability benchmarks for the Heretic-edited checkpoints.
Tests Heretic’s direction-estimation/edit-search attack and a trained defense against that search; it does not test training specifically against direct activation ablation.
Global versus per-layer attack scopes are compared, but the study does not test whether refusal is represented by multiple directions, a cone, or an affine set.
Does not separate harmfulness judgments from refusal decisions.
Does not test transfer across languages, base/instruct variants, or other model variants as a direction-transfer question.
Does not compare refusal-training methods or training stages to determine whether they produce a removable direction.

relation.reason: Its own baseline Heretic results on four undefended models, and on defended checkpoints, bear on whether abliteration removes refusal.

tranche.reason: Heretic is an Optuna search over difference-of-means projection edits (a different method from Arditi weight orthogonalization). The study reports harmful-prompt refusal on undefended and defended released models, so it bears on V2.

source_check.notes: Rows T3-{Q4B,Q8B,G1B,G12B}-K1000-base still hold the four-model mean 3.75; the per-model values are 5/8/2/0. No unedited refusal rate is given for any model: all values are minimum refusals over 200 Heretic trials. Several rows remain linked to V3 although the verdict fix drops it. The extracted text misplaces the captions of appendix Tables 5-7; matching on content, the first table is overall, the second per-layer and the third global. The text calls all four models instruction models, so Qwen3-8B's 'not stated' type should be 'instruct'.
